Bitta, the then President of Indian Youth Congress (I) at 5, Raisina Road, New Delhi, resulting in the death of nine people and injuries to several others. Devender Pal Singh, a member of KLF, a terrorist organization, was arrested at the Indira Gandhi International Airport on 19 January 1995, after being deported from Germany. He was charged under Section 3(2)(i) of the Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act, 1987 (TADA) and Sections 120B, 302, 307, 326, 324, 323, 436, and 427 of the Indian Penal Code for his involvement in the bomb blast.

He then filed a special leave petition before the Supreme Court, which was also dismissed. The case was then remanded to the trial court for confirmation of the death sentence.

The trial court confirmed the death sentence, and Devender Pal Singh filed another criminal appeal before the Delhi High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the death sentence. Devender Pal Singh then filed a special leave petition before the Supreme Court, which was also dismissed.

The Supreme Court, while dismissing the special leave petition, observed that the collective conscience of the community was shocked by the brutal, grotesque, diabolical, revolting, and dastardly manner in which the bomb blast was carried out. The court held that the crime was enormous in proportion and that the victim of the murder was an innocent child, a helpless woman, or an old or infirm person, or a person vis-a-vis whom the murderer was in a dominating position, or a public figure generally loved and respected by the community.

The court held that the accused deserved the death penalty, and the death sentence was confirmed.

In conclusion, the Supreme Court upheld the death sentence awarded to Devender Pal Singh for his involvement in the bomb blast outside the office of Mr. S. Bitta, the then President of Indian Youth Congress (I) at 5, Raisina Road, New Delhi, on 11 September 1993. The court observed that the crime was committed in a brutal and dastardly manner, and that the accused deserved the death penalty.

Facts: The appellant company, Bhopal Sugar Industries, Limited, carried on the business of manufacturing and selling sugar in various grades and quantities. It had its factory at Sehore which was formerly in the Bhopal State and is now situated in the State of Madhya Pradesh. It purchased sugar-cane from local cultivators and also grew its own sugar-cane in farms situate in that State, such sugar-cane being used for its manufacture of sugar. During the year of account ending on September 30, 1950, the appellant company purchased 7,72,217 maunds of sugar-cane from local cultivators at various purchasing centers, 14 in number, situated at a distance of about to 22 miles from its factory. The price paid was Rs.1-4-6 per maund, that being the price fixed by the then State of Bhopal. The average cost of transporting the sugar-cane from the various centers to the factory was stated to be Rs.0-4-9 per maund. During the same period, the appellant company grew its own sugar-cane to the extent of 6,78,490 maunds and brought the same along with the cultivators sugar-cane to its factory for manufacturing sugar. For the sugar-cane grown on its own farms, the appellant company claimed Rs.1-13-0 per maund as its market value (including Rs.0-4-9 as average transport charges), the total market value for 6,78,490 maunds thus coming to Rs.12,29,763. The appellant company deducted from the aforesaid, market value sum of Rs.9,77,772 as agricultural expenses, namely, expenses of harvesting, loading, etc., and claimed the balance of Rs.2,51,991 as agricultural income to be deducted from the computation of its total income for the assessment year 1951-52.

Issues: The issue before the court was whether the learned Judicial Commissioner of Bhopal rightly dismissed petition under Article 226 of the Constitution made by the Bhopal Sugar Industries, Limited, praying for the issue of an appropriate order or direction in the nature of writ of mandamus to compel the Income-tax Officer, Bhopal, respondent herein, to carry-out certain directions given by the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal, Bombay, to the said officer in an appeal preferred by the appellant company from an order of assessment made against it by the respondent.

Statute: The Income-tax Act, 1961

Ratio of the decision: The court held that the refusal to carry out the directions which a superior tribunal had given in exercise of its appellate powers was in effect denial of justice and was furthermore destructive of one of the basic principles in the administration of justice based as it is in this country on hierarchy of courts. The result of such refusal would lead to chaos in the administration of justice.

Ruling by Present Court (Decision): The court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Judicial Commissioner. The court directed the Income-tax Officer to carry out the directions given by the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal, Bombay, in the appeal preferred by the appellant company from an order of assessment made against it by the respondent.

Conclusion: The court upheld the principle that subordinate tribunal must carry out the directions of superior tribunal. The court rejected the argument of learned counsel for the respondent that the order of the Tribunal was unintelligible and that the respondent did his best to understand it according to his light. The court found no difficulty in understanding the order of the Tribunal and directed the respondent to ascertain the average transport charges per maund from the centers to the factory and add to it the rate of Rs.1-4-6 per maund of sugar-cane. The court also directed the Income-tax Officer to work out the market value of the sugar-cane grown by the appellant company in its own farms on that basis.
